Organizing 2024 data for bar charts
This code calculates the average number of offensive plays per game for each Big Ten football team during the 2024 season. It groups the game log data by conference and team, sums each team’s total plays, counts the number of games played, and divides total plays by games to find the average. Finally, it filters the results to include only Big Ten teams and keeps the conference name, team name, and average plays for analysis or visualization.

big_ten_2024 <- logs_2024 |> 
  group_by(Conference, Team) |> 
  summarise (
    TeamPlays = sum(TotalPlays),
    Games = n_distinct(Gtm)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    AvgPlays = TeamPlays/Games
  ) |> 
  select (Conference, Team, AvgPlays) |> 
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference")

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Conference'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.




Making the 2024 Average Plays Bar Chart for Big Ten teams
This code uses ggplot to create a bar chart that compares Big Ten football teams by their average number of offensive plays per game in 2024. Each bar represents one team, with the length of the bar showing its average plays. The teams are reordered so that those with higher or lower averages appear in order. The chart includes a clear title and labeled axes for readability, and the coord_flip() function turns it horizontal so team names are easier to read. Overall, it provides a simple visual comparison of offensive tempo across Big Ten teams.

ggplot() +
  geom_bar(
    data=big_ten_2024,
    aes(x=reorder(Team, AvgPlays),
        weight=AvgPlays)) +
  labs(
    title="Big Ten Schools By Number of Plays Ran 2024",
    x="School",
    y="Average Number of Plays") +
  coord_flip()










Organizing 2025 data for bar charts
This code calculates the average number of offensive plays per game for each Big Ten football team during the 2025 season. It groups the 2025 game log data by conference and team, sums each team’s total offensive plays, and counts how many games they played. Then, it divides total plays by the number of games to find each team’s average plays per game. Finally, it filters the results to include only teams from the Big Ten Conference and selects the relevant columns — conference, team, and average plays — for further analysis or visualization.

big_ten_2025 <- logs_2025 |> 
  group_by(Conference, Team) |> 
  summarise (
    TeamPlays = sum(TotalPlays),
    Games = n_distinct(Gtm)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    AvgPlays = TeamPlays/Games
  ) |> 
  select (Conference, Team, AvgPlays) |> 
  filter(Conference == "Big Ten Conference")

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Conference'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.




Making the 2025 Average Plays Bar Chart for Big Ten teams
This code creates a horizontal bar chart showing the average number of offensive plays per game for each Big Ten football team in the 2025 season. Using ggplot, it plots each team’s average plays as a bar and orders the teams based on their averages for easier comparison. The labs() function adds a descriptive title and axis labels, while coord_flip() rotates the chart so team names are displayed vertically for better readability. Overall, the visualization clearly highlights how offensive tempo varies among Big Ten teams during the 2025 season.

ggplot() +
  geom_bar(
    data=big_ten_2025,
    aes(x=reorder(Team, AvgPlays),
        weight=AvgPlays)) +
  labs(
    title="Big Ten Schools By Number of Plays Ran 2025",
    x="School",
    y="Average Number of Plays") +
  coord_flip()








The biggest thing I notice is that Maryland ran the most average plays in the Big Ten last year, which is quite surprising given how poor they were on offense with Billy Edwards Jr. under center. Maryland was in the bottom half in average scoring last season, producing 30 points a game — good for 10th-most in the Big Ten. Maryland’s defense was one of the worst in the conference too, making it confusing how they ran so many plays. It most likely relates to the fact that Maryland went up-tempo often last season.
In terms of across the conference, the average number of plays has gone up slightly, but that might still be weighed heavily by nonconference play. When are you playing inferior opponents, you are able to run more plays since your opponents are typically not scoring many points or sustaining drives. Something that surprises me is how far down the top Big Ten football programs are this season, like Ohio State and Illinois who are both top 10 opponents.

maryland_volleyball <- volleyball_data |> 
  filter(team == "Maryland") |> 
  summarise (
    total_kills = sum(kills),
    total_blocks = sum(block_solos + (block_assists/2)),
    total_aces = sum(aces),
    total_opp_errors = sum(defensive_errors)
  )


md <- c("Kills"=525, "Blocks"=114, "Aces"=75, "Opponents Errors"=257,332)


nebraska_volleyball <- volleyball_data |> 
  filter(team == "Nebraska") |> 
  summarise (
    total_kills = sum(kills),
    total_blocks = sum(block_solos + (block_assists/2)),
    total_aces = sum(aces),
    total_opp_errors = sum(defensive_errors)
  )


neb <- c("Kills"=777, "Blocks"=141, "Aces"=60, "Opponents Errors"=325)


iron(
 waffle(md/2, 
        rows = 10, 
        title="Maryland's point distribution", 
        xlab="1 square = 1 point", 
        colors = c("black", "red", "yellow", "grey", "white")
        ),
 waffle(neb/2, 
        rows = 10, 
        title="Nebraska's point distribution", 
        xlab="1 square = 1 point",
        colors = c("black", "red", "yellow", "grey")
        )
)








Maryland produced 971 total points, with most coming from kills (525 points, 54%) and opponent errors (257 points, 26%). The Terps also added 114 points from blocks (12%) and 75 from aces (8%). Their scoring profile shows a team that often relies on defensive opportunities and opponent mistakes rather than generating points through consistent offensive pressure.
Nebraska, the top-ranked team in the nation, recorded 1,303 points, driven by a dominant 777 kills (60%), along with 141 blocks (11%), 60 aces (5%), and 325 opponent errors (25%).
The contrast reflects the gap between one of the country’s elite programs and a Maryland squad still trying to find its footing near the bottom of the Big Ten. Nebraska’s attack is self-sustaining and explosive, generating points through high-efficiency kills and balanced play at the net. Maryland, meanwhile, leans more on opponent miscues, underscoring the difference between a national contender and a rebuilding conference opponent.

Penn State’s ground game was one of the best in the country last season, led by its two-headed monster of Nicholas Singleton and Kaytron Allen. The duo aided the Nittany Lions to over 200 rushing yards a game as part of their journey to the College Football Playoffs Semifinals. While Penn State has produced NFL running back talent like Saquon Barkley and Miles Sanders, the program has struggled on the ground over the past decade.
Since 2015, the Nittany Lions have had 15 wins in which they’ve rushed for fewer than 100 yards — the fourth-most of all Division I teams. Penn State has totalled that number over 137 games for the eighth-highest percentage in the country (10.95 percent). This percentage is the fifth-best compared to Power Five schools, closely behind Big Ten foe Purdue. While these kinds of performances are rare across college football — the national average is 5.06 percent — the Nittany Lions have proven they can win games primarily through the air.
Despite having Saquon Barkley in the backfield for three seasons, Penn State won eight games with less than 100 rushing yards from 2015 to 2017. But 2021 was the highest total. With Sean Clifford under center, the signal caller threw for over 3,000 passing yards and guided the Nittany Lions to a seven-win total. Four of those games featured Penn State’s rush attack combining for under 100 yards. Operating without a clear top running back, the Nittany Lions struggled on the ground, putting more stress on Clifford to march the offense down the field.
While the style of football is shifting more towards mobile quarterbacks that can extend plays and scramble, there have still been 58 instances this season of teams who won the game with under 100 rushing yards. New Mexico State has the most this season, with three such performances. Half of Maryland’s 2025 campaign wins have been reliant on Malik Washington and the Terps’ passing game. This is a concerning sign for Maryland heading into its final fives games of the regular season, which features a pair of ranked clashes.

Comparing the last 11 seasons of Maryland football
text:
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  offense defense
    <dbl>   <dbl>
1    5.76    5.63











Malik Washington — the nation’s fifth-ranked quarterback in the class of 2025 — was expected to be head coach Michael Locksley’s prized possession that helped put Maryland football back on the map. After Taulia Tagovailoa graduated in 2023 and the Terps underwent a rebuilding season in 2024, expectations were high for the true freshman quarterback heading into the 2025 campaign.
Through the first four games, he didn’t disappoint. Washington threw for 1,038 yards and eight passing touchdowns while also adding two rushing scores. Maryland went into its first bye week still unbeaten and with reason for optimism ahead of the meat of its Big Ten schedule.
But it’s quickly spiraled out. The Terps are on a four-game losing streak and their chances of bowl eligibility have gotten slimmer and slimmer every week. Washington has thrown four picks and fumbled once during this rough stretch, including a three-turnover performance against Indiana.
A big part of Maryland’s losing streak has been its poor offensive performances. While the Terps’ defense has been solid throughout the season — they have allowed the third-fewest yards per play of any Maryland team over the last 11 seasons — the offense has been scuffling. Maryland’s offense was expected to take a step forward this season, but it has produced the program’s second-fewest yards per play since 2015. Some of these struggles can be attributed to Washington only being a freshman, but with Locksley under pressure and in desperate need of a win, the Terps will have to quickly right the ship in the final four games.

title: Comparing NFL teams EPA from week 3 of the 2022 season to week 9
text:
Process
To replicate the ESPN analysis of red zone success, I used the nflreadr package to load NFL play-by-play data and focused on all offensive plays that occurred inside the opponent’s 20-yard line (yardline_100 < 21). Plays such as penalties, kneel-downs, and spikes were excluded to ensure only true offensive plays contributed to expected points added (EPA).
For each team, I calculated total red zone plays and total EPA through Week 3 and then through Week 9 of the 2025 season. These summaries were joined and visualized using a dumbbell chart — each line shows how a team’s total red zone EPA has changed over that span, with green points representing Week 3 and blue points representing Week 9. Teams are ordered by their total Week 9 EPA to highlight overall performance and improvement across the season.

title: Comparing NFL teams EPA from week 3 of the 2022 season to week 9
text:
Conclusions
The results show clear tiers of red zone efficiency and development as the season has progressed.
Biggest Improvers: The Philadelphia Eagles stand out as the team that improved the most, jumping from 0 total EPA in Week 3 to over +20 EPA by Week 9. That surge reflects sharper red zone execution, particularly their increased touchdown conversion rate and consistent quarterback play. The Minnesota Vikings and Cleveland Browns also showed notable improvement, moving from slightly negative early-season numbers to strong positive totals by midseason.
Consistently Strong Teams: The Kansas City Chiefs have been dominant throughout, leading the entire league in total red zone EPA after nine weeks. Their early-season efficiency continued without much regression, showing how stable their offense remains in high-leverage scoring situations. The Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys also maintained steady, above-average performance in both timeframes.
Teams That Fell Off: A few teams have seen their red zone performance decline. The Buffalo Bills and Green Bay Packers both started with solid early-season numbers but saw little or no improvement, slipping in overall ranking as other offenses surged ahead.
Consistent Struggles: At the bottom of the chart, the Denver Broncos, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and Indianapolis Colts have struggled all season, remaining in negative EPA territory through both Week 3 and Week 9. Their lack of progress indicates deeper offensive inefficiencies, especially in play design and execution near the goal line.

Throughout the season, Maryland has been among the worst rushing teams in the Big Ten, struggling to generate consistent production on the ground. The Terps have leaned heavily on their passing attack, often abandoning the run when drives stall or game scripts turn against them. Their data point sits well below the Big Ten average in both rushing yards per game and yards per carry, a clear indicator of inefficiency. In a conference built on trench play and time of possession, Maryland’s inability to establish a ground presence has been one of its most defining weaknesses.
That’s why last week’s performance against Rutgers stood out as such an anomaly. For the first time all season, Maryland looked dominant in the run game, posting one of the highest yards-per-carry averages in the Big Ten that week. They broke tackles, sustained blocks, and controlled tempo — all the hallmarks of a team in command. Yet the Terps lost. Across both the Big Ten and the national scene, that kind of result is exceptionally rare. Teams that rush for that many yards per carry almost always win; nationally, that level of rushing efficiency has translated into victory nearly every time. Maryland’s loss was one of the few exceptions.
That outcome underscores how fragile Maryland’s season has been — even when they finally solved one of their biggest problems, other issues surfaced. The data reaffirm that rushing efficiency remains one of the most reliable predictors of success in college football, especially in a league defined by physicality like the Big Ten. Maryland’s showing against Rutgers was a glimpse of what their offense could be, but it also highlighted how small the margin for error remains. In a conference where running the ball still defines identity, Maryland’s rare outlier serves as both a warning and a what-if.

Grouping the beeswarm plot by class year — freshmen through seniors — and filtering to players with at least five shots on goal revealed a scoring landscape where the Big Ten sits unmistakably near the top. With each class forming its own horizontal band, the top ten Big Ten goalscorers consistently appeared at the very top of their year clusters, showing how the conference produces elite finishers across the entire developmental timeline. No one embodied that better than Indiana’s senior Palmer Ault, whose goals-per-game rate wasn’t merely strong—it placed him at the peak of the senior band nationally, a reminder of how dangerous Big Ten strikers can become by the end of their careers.
To add national context, UCLA’s Sergi Solans — the country’s standout sophomore goalscorer — was layered onto the chart. Solans sat right at the ceiling of the sophomore band, defining elite efficiency for his class. What made the comparison revealing wasn’t that Solans outpaced others, but that multiple Big Ten scorers across different years sat right behind him within their own groups. Even when separating the swarm by class, the Big Ten still packed the upper edges of every band, reinforcing that its offensive dominance isn’t tied to a single superstar pipeline — it’s a conference-wide pattern.
Overlaying Maryland’s attackers only strengthened that story. Their top scorers didn’t scatter across the middle of the distribution; they settled directly in the same upper scoring zones where the Big Ten’s best lived. Maryland fit naturally into a league defined by high-end finishing talent and experienced attackers driving production. The beeswarm made the message clear: whether you look at seniors like Ault, national standouts like Solans, or Maryland’s own scoring core, the Big Ten remains one of the most potent attacking conferences in Division I soccer—dangerous in every class year, and dangerous in every match.

If there’s anything we’ve learned from Buzz Williams’ previous stops (Marquette, Virginia Tech and Marquette), it’s that his teams typically get a steady diet of points at the free-throw line, feast on the offensive glass and play strong defense. But this season, only one of those traits has shown up.
While there was expected to be a bit of a grace period with Buzz Williams’ arrival in College Park and an entirely new team built in nearly a month, the first five games have been anything but pretty. The Terps barely beat a usually strong Marquette team, eked past Mount St. Mary’s in overtime, and needed second-half surges to beat Coppin State and Alcorn State. Maryland also looked extremely outmatched in its home-opener against Georgetown, arguably its worst performance of the season.
Injuries have certainly taken their toll on the team. Myles Rice has played in just one game, Pharrel Payne suffered what appeared to be a gruesome injury against Marquette (rumor is he is available to play in the Players Era Tournament), George Turkson missed a pair of games and Solomon Washington has yet to make his Terps’ debut.
But still, Maryland has struggled in two of the three areas that are usually staples with Buzz Williams.
Despite the Terps’ offensive struggles this season — Maryland is shooting just 25 percent from deep if you take away Diggy Coit’s numbers and just over 42 percent from the field — free throws have been their saving grace. Maryland has gotten to the line at an unprecedented rate (32.6 times per game and knocking down 82.2 percent), which has fueled its victories. Darius Adams is the leader of that group. While the true freshman hasn’t found his shot yet, he has gotten fouled seemingly every time he attacks the basket.
But Maryland has struggled significantly on the glass this season. Even with Pharrel Payne in the lineup, the Terps lack someone who can consistenly corral rebounds. It only got exponentially worse with Payne out of the lineup against Mount St. Mary’s. Maryland was outrebounded in that game and gave up 12 offensive rebounds. The Terps have recorded the third-fewest rebounds per game over the last 11 seasons and only trail the 2023-24 team in opponents rebounds — not a good section of the scatterplot to be in. Maryland also hasn’t gotten enough second-chance opportunities to make up for its poor offense.
The most concerning thing has been the Terps’ defense through five games. Maryland has allowed 73.4 points per game this season — significantly more than any of its teams throughout the last 11 seasons. The Terps have allowed opponents to get to the rim at ease this season, which is why Buzz Williams made an adjustment heading into their game against Mount St. Mary’s. Unfortunately, the Mountaineers couldn’t miss from deep. Mount St. Mary’s scored 90 points in the overtime loss.
While its a short sample size, Maryland fans should feel a bit concerned heading into the Players Era Tournament.

Using team-level data from the past decade, I built three visual comparisons to evaluate the defining traits of Buzz Williams’ teams across his tenures at Virginia Tech and Texas A&M. After summarizing per-game team statistics—such as offensive rebounds, total rebounds, free-throw attempts, and shooting percentages — I isolated the seasons Williams coached and compared them to the national landscape. Plotting his teams in red against all other Division I teams in grey made it easy to identify which traits consistently separated Buzz’s teams from typical programs.
Those visualizations reveal a clear identity. Williams’ best teams have almost always dominated the offensive glass, especially at Texas A&M, where several squads ranked among the nation’s most aggressive rebounding units. The 2023–24 Aggies in particular stood out as one of the strongest offensive-rebounding teams of the entire decade. His teams also consistently won the free-throw battle, often attempting significantly more free throws than their opponents. This combination of second-chance opportunities and trips to the line became a reliable scoring formula, especially in seasons when his teams struggled to shoot from the perimeter.
The third plot highlights the biggest contrast within Williams’ coaching career: his Virginia Tech teams shot the ball extremely well from three, while his Texas A&M teams did not. In College Station, Williams leaned overwhelmingly on rebounding, physicality and free-throw generation to compensate for inefficient perimeter shooting. Even his best A&M teams were subpar from deep and below average from the field overall, relying instead on sheer volume of possessions and paint pressure to score.
Maryland’s early-season profile does not yet line up with that established formula. Much like last season — when the Terps routinely lost rebounding battles and ranked near the bottom of the Big Ten on the glass — the current group has again struggled to secure rebounds through the first five games. Their issues extend to shooting as well: Maryland has opened the season poorly from deep and from the field, often going minutes without a bucket.
The one area in which Maryland does resemble a typical Buzz Williams team is at the free-throw line. Despite their shooting and rebounding problems, the Terps have gotten to the line at a high rate through their first five games, generating much of their offense through physical downhill attacks. Still, when paired with their current struggles on the boards and from deep, that alone hasn’t been enough to produce convincing performances. If Maryland is going to grow into the identity that has carried Williams’ previous teams, improvement on the glass—paired with at least marginally better shooting will be essential as the season progresses.

ggplot() + geom_point(data=lineups_filtered, aes(x=min, y=plus_minus)) +
labs(
  title="The Wizards best lineup features a mix of veteran and young players", 
  subtitle="Two veterans, two second-year players and a rookie compose Washington's most productive lineup",
  x="Minutes played together", 
  y="Each lineup's plus/minus") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=best_and_worst_lineup, 
    aes(x=min, y=plus_minus, label=group_name))








The Wizards, tied for the fewest wins in the league, continue to navigate a long-term rebuild centered around developing young pieces. Because of that, their early-season lineup data offers a revealing look at which combinations actually work and which ones still need major adjustment. The gap between Washington’s strongest and weakest units is stark, emphasizing how volatile a rebuilding roster can be.
The most effective lineup features Khris Middleton, CJ McCollum, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, and Tre Johnson, and it currently boasts an impressive +22 plus/minus. This group succeeds because it blends veteran leadership with emerging talent. Middleton and McCollum bring structure, shot creation, and calm decision-making, while Sarr anchors the interior with length and mobility. George and Johnson provide energy, defensive versatility, and off-ball movement, giving the Wizards one of their few lineups that consistently elevates the team’s overall efficiency.
Offensively, this positive group works because of its spacing and balance. Middleton and McCollum demand defensive attention, freeing Sarr as a roller and allowing George and Johnson to attack closeouts or connect plays. They generate clean looks, limit turnovers, and maintain rhythm—something the Wizards struggle to do with more developmental lineups. Their +22 mark reflects possessions that feel purposeful and connected rather than improvised.
On the opposite end of the spectrum, the worst-performing lineup—Marvin Bagley III, Corey Kispert, Cam Whitmore, Kyshawn George, and Tre Johnson—holds a troubling –25 plus/minus. This unit noticeably lacks a true initiator, often relying on difficult shots late in the clock. Bagley’s interior-focused game clashes with Whitmore’s slashing, and without a stabilizing veteran presence, the offense stalls. The spacing becomes cramped, the ball sticks, and quality attempts become rare.
Defensively, the issues grow even more pronounced. Without a rim-protecting big or a defensive leader, this lineup frequently allows uncontested drives, miscommunicates on switches, and gives up second-chance points. The –25 differential reflects not just missed shots, but structural problems on both ends. Taken together, the difference between Washington’s best and worst lineups shows why a young, rebuilding team tied for the fewest wins is still searching for combinations that offer stability and long-term promise.
